opening_message:
Ticket 1: Robert Weber (employee ID E047) requests admin access to Source Code.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E047.
Note 1 (ticket 1), written by HR agent:
  - role: Payroll Specialist (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: write
  - comment: Robert Weber (E047), full-time Payroll Specialist, requests admin on Source Code. Full-time employees max at write unless their role owns the system; Payroll Specialist does not own Source Code, so admin is not permitted. Recommend write.
Note 2 (ticket 1), written by Security agent:
  - role: Payroll Specialist (not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1 by HR agent)
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: read
  - comment: Security DB shows Robert Weber (E047) is a contractor with basic security training. Contractors never get admin; with basic training the max is read. Requested admin, so recommend read.
reason: Robert Weber (E047) requested admin on Source Code. Per HR's authoritative employment record, he is a full-time Payroll Specialist. Full-time employees max at write unless their role owns the system; Payroll Specialist does not own Source Code (Engineer does), so admin is not permitted and the maximum is write. Requested admin exceeds the maximum, so per policy the maximum (write) is granted. Note: Security's note classified him as a contractor with basic training (which would cap at read), but HR's verified employment-type record is the authoritative source for employment status.

content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket.

Employee: Robert Weber (E047)
Request: admin access to Source Code

Notes:
- HR agent: role Payroll Specialist, employment type full_time, recommendation write. Says full-time employees max at write unless role owns system; Payroll Specialist doesn't own Source Code, so admin not permitted. Recommend write.
- Security agent: role Payroll Specialist (not verified), employment type contractor (looked up), security training basic, recommendation read. Contractors never admin; basic training max read.

Discrepancy: HR says full_time, Security says contractor.

The access policy:
1. full_time employees: up to write. Admin only if role owns system.
2. contractor employees: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin.

If full_time (HR): max write (Payroll Specialist doesn't own Source Code). Requested admin > write, grant write.
If contractor (Security): max read (basic training). Grant read.

Which to use? The notes differ on employment type. HR looked up employment type in own database. Security looked up employment type in own database. Both claim lookup. Hmm.

As Approver, I need to decide. Which source is more reliable? The HR agent is typically the source for employment type (full_time vs contractor). The Security agent looked up in their own database too. There's a conflict.

Typically in these scenarios, the HR agent's employment data is authoritative for employment status. But the Security agent also looked up. Hmm.

Let me consider the policy: full-time employees max write unless role owns system. Payroll Specialist does not own Source Code (Engineer owns it). So max for full-time = write. If contractor = read (basic training).

Given conflict, I should probably rely on HR for employment type since HR manages employment records. HR recommendation: write. Security recommendation: read.

The safest approach: The employee's facts from HR (full_time) support write. Security says contractor -> read. Which to trust?

In such scenarios, I think the HR agent's employment type is authoritative because HR database is the source of truth for employment type. The Security agent may have stale data. HR note says "looked up in own database before writing" for employment type. Security also said looked up in own database. Both claim lookup, so both are "verified" from their own DBs.

Hmm. This is a classic conflict scenario. The team memory notes say HR looked up employment type in own database. Security looked up employment type in own database too, but got contractor. So there is a direct contradiction between two databases.

How to resolve? Perhaps the policy says employment type - HR is the authority. Typically HR owns employment status. I'll go with HR: full-time employee, Payroll Specialist. Max write. Requested admin. Grant write.

Wait - but the role: HR says Payroll Specialist. Security says Payroll Specialist (not looked up, same as HR). So role consistent: Payroll Specialist. Payroll Specialist does not own Source Code, so admin not allowed; full-time max write.

Security training: basic (from Security DB). For contractor, basic training max read. But we determined full-time per HR.

Decision: write.

Let me submit write with reason citing HR employment type full-time, role Payroll Specialist does not own Source Code, so max write; requested admin exceeds max, grant write (policy grants max when request above max). Note the disagreement with Security's contractor classification, but HR is authoritative for employment type. Actually should I mention? I'll provide evidence.

I'll submit decision: write.
